2. The respondents in those appeals are different companies which are registered importers under the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1950, hereinafter referred to as "the Act of 1950" and they are industrial consumers having approved entitlement for import of raw materials for which they were issued with pass books under the aforesaid Act to enable them to import the necessary raw materials and to help them open necessary letters of credit. 

 10. In their affidavit before the High Court which was filed before Act III of 1967 was passed the appellants state that since the year 1961-62 procurement of iron and steel under US AID loan had been confined to the USA only where prices were at least 40% higher for individual items in comparison to world prices. As a measure of price stabilisation the import of iron and steel from the USA was consequently subsidised from the counterpart funds to the extent of the difference between the US and the non-US prices. From November 20, 1962 this subsidy was withdrawn, since then the imports from the USA continued to be made at their original price. As a result of the postponement of the Consortium Meeting in July, 1965, US AID Loan for the import of iron and steel and other commodities was not available. The Government, therefore, decided to import some major items of iron and steel under its own cash resources. These imports were considerably cheaper than those from the USA. Since the trade and industries in Pakistan were maintaining the price level for iron and steel products on the basis of imports from the USA and stock at the higher prices-were still in the pipeline, the Government decided to impose a price differential on cheaper imports for the purpose of price equalization so that the interests of the trade and industries may be safeguarded and discrimination between those who imported iron and steel from the USA at higher prices and those who imposed under cash from elsewhere maybe avoided. It was denied that the price differential was a tax so as to require legislative sanction. Further, a price differential was introduced as a measure of control to regulate the import and export of certain commodities in exercise of the powers under Section 3(1) of the Imports and Exports Control Act, 1950. The object was not to collect funds for public purposes but to equalise prices of the iron and steel. 

 13. The Writ Petitions were heard by a Division Bench of the High Court which, by their judgment delivered on February 2, 1968 made the Rule absolute and declared the impugned notifications relating to differential to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect. Also, directions were given to refund the money already realised by the Government from the respondents. It was held (1) that the Act of 1950 was not a fiscal statute so as to authorise the imposition of a tax, (2) that the Import Policy Order which was issued in exercise of the powers conferred by Section 3 (1) of the Act of 1950 did not authorise the Central Government to levy any imposition of the nature of price differential, (3) that the piece differential surcharge is a tax or duty which can be levied only under a fiscal statute. (4) that the Act III of 1967 is a valid piece of legislation and the levy of the price equalisation surcharge by it is in conformity with the provisions of Article 48 of the Constitution and also within entry 43(a) of the Third Schedule of the Constitution, (5) that though the requirement of the national interest of Pakistan was not mentioned in the Act III of 1967, this omission did not affect the validity of the Act, (6) that while enacting Act III of 1997 the Central Legislature did not abdicate its essential legislative function, (7) that for an effective application of Act III of 1967 it is necessary that Rules should have been framed as provided in Section 6 of the Act, particularly with regard to assessment and payment of the price equalisation surcharge, (8) that section 7 of Act III of 1967 must be strictly construed, (9), that Section 7 only validated such levy as was made by or in pursuance of S.R.O 49 (R)/66 dated 23-4-66 or by order under any Rule, order, notification or other Instrument made or issued under the Act of 19 50, and (10) that the demand to furnish Bank guarantee having been made in pursuance of public notice and not under the aforesaid S.R.O. 49 (R)/66 or the act of 1950 is not validated under Section 7 or Act III of 1967. 

 14. Mr. K. A Bakr, Attorney-General for Bangladesh, appeared for the appellants and submitted that under Section 3(1) of the Act of 1950, the Central Government was authorised to make the above mentioned impositions and the impugned Import Policy Order and the various public notices thereunder making such impositions were, therefore, validly made. Next, he submitted that the main question involved in these appeals require determination of the legislative competence of the Central legislature in enacting Act III of 1967 which under Section 3 of the Act, sought to make legal the imposition of price equalisation surcharge on specified goods imported in any shipping period after April 22, 1966 and under Section 7 of the act legalised retrospectively price differential levied and collected/or purported o have been levied and collected, by or in pursuance of the notification No.SRO-49(R)/66. So for as retrospective validation under section 7 is concerned, the learned Attorney General submitted that the finding of the High Court that "Section 7 of the Act does not operate to legalise retrospectively the said price differential" was wrong. 

 First, in referring to the Import and Export (Control) Act, 1950, it was submitted, that it did not authorise the imposition of the price differential which is not a fee for service rendered, but a tax and it, therefore, required necessary legislative authorisation. AS the Act itself did not provide such authorisation, the Import Policy Order No.SRO 49(R)/66 and the public Notices issued thereunder could not authorise such imposition. 

 21. To proceed chronologically so as to understand the contents of the various Acts, Order and Public Notices made thereunder, reference may first be made to the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1950 (Act No.XXXIX of 1950). This Act conferred the power upon the Central Government to prohibit or control imports and exports into and from Pakistan and was to remain in force for a period of twenty years. As Section 3 which contains the substantive power to prohibit, restrict or otherwise control imports-info and exports from Pakistan may be relevant for our purpose, it is quoted below: 

 22. Neither in this or any other section of the Act any reference is found to the power of the Government to levy price equalisation surcharge as imposed by Act III of 1967. The respondents complied with the provisions of this Act and also of the Licences and Permits Order, 1958 which was issued in pursuance of the Act. It was, therefore, contended that the Import Policy Order which was issued in pursuance of this Act namely, SRO 49(R)/66 cannot therefore, authorise the Central Government to levy an imposition in the nature of price differential since the Act merely enables the Government to prohibit, restrict or otherwise control the import of goods and regulate all practices and procedure Connected therewith. Neither was the imposition of the levy was procedural. The levy of price equalisation surcharge which was imposed by the Import Policy Order was substantive taxation being not auhorised by the Act of 1950 was beyond the pale of the authority of the Government. 

 27. The Government issued these orders in exercise of it’s power under Section 3(1) of the Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1950. These Orders were followed up by various Public Notices issued by the Chief Controller of Imports and Exports, Government of Pakistan. 

 33. The validity of the impugned Government action in so far as it is sought to be justified by relying upon the Act of 1950 and the various Import Policy Orders and Public Notices just quoted above may first be looked into before considering Act III of 1967 which was enacted to validate them much later than the dates upon which they were issued. 

 34. On a consideration of the provisions of Section 3(1) of the Act of 1950 and of the amended paragraph 23(iii) of the Import Policy Order, it becomes apparent that none of these provisions authorises the imposition of price differential surcharges which was made for the first time by Notification No. SRO-49(R) 66 issued on April 23, 1966. Though, of course, it was argued quite persistently that the provisions of the Act do authorise such imposition of price differential surcharge, the question has arisen whether from the very nature of the imposition which bears no resemblance to fees chargeable for services rendered, it can be termed a fee or it is a tax. For on reference to the provisions of Section 3(1) it is seen to have merely authorised charging of fees for issuing licences, permits, letters of credit etc. 

 35. In support of the contention that it was tax, and not fee reference was made to the cases, namely Main Land Dairy Products Sales Adjustment Committee Vs. Crystal Dairy Ltd., (1933) AC 168; Attorney General Vs. Wills United Dairies (1921) 37 T.L.R. 884. Since price differential surcharge was required to be paid in addition to the C.I.F. value, bank charges, inspection fee etc. and to be calculated on a certain basis and in the manner laid down in item (2) of SRO-49(R)66 it possesses the characteristics of a tax. Had the surcharge been not a tax but it partook of the nature of a fee, it’s imposition under the aforesaid Import Policy Order issued in exercise of the powers under Section 3(1) of the Act, 1950, would have been legal. Since the surcharge appears to be a tax, its imposition was not authorised by this Act which, besides being not a fiscal statute, did not, as appears from its provisioners, confer the power to tax upon a named authority. As observed by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, taxation to be effective must be imposed by clear words. Vide Royal Trust Co. Vs. Minister of Finance, A.I.R. 1921 P.C. 184. As the Act itself did not confer the power to tax, no authority or officer of the executive can impose a tax claiming the jurisdiction to do so by invoking it. The Import Policy Order, namely, SRO-49(R)/66, therefore, seems to have been issued without jurisdiction. Nor, as already seen, the jurisdiction to make the imposition is conferred by paragraph 23(iii) of SRO No. 65(R)/66. Even if, in fact, it did, this would have been equally invalid because Section 3(1) of the Act of 1950 did not authorize the Government to do so. The intention of the Legislature to impose the surcharge cannot be inferred from the language used in this Section. The result would be that the claim of the chief Controller of Imports and Exports to impose the price equalisation surcharge by issuing the public notices concerned must, also, therefore, fail, because the validity of the public notices are dependent on that of the SRO-49(R) 66. 

 (3) Whoever fails or neglects to comply with any direction under sub-section (2) shall be deemed to have contravened the provisions of the Imports and Exports (Control) Act of 1950, and shall be punishable under Section 5 of that Act." 

 "7. Validation.- The price differential levied and collected or purported to have been levied and collected, by or in pursuance of the Ministry of Commerce Notification No.SRO 49(R)/66 dated the 23rd April, 1966 or by or under any rule, order, notification or other instrument made or issued under the Import and Exports (Control) Act, 1950 (XXXIX of 1950), shall subject to necessary adjustments, be deemed to have been levied and collected as price equalization surcharge end the goods on which such price differential has been levied shall be deemed to have been declared to be specified goods as if this Act were in force at the time when such price differential was levied and collected." 

 78. As regards the ex-post-facto validation of the price equalisation surcharge which was imposed to the enactment of Act III of 1967, the provisions of section 7 as quoted earlier show that it sought to validate only such price differential surcharge as already levied and collected or purported to have been levied and collected by or in pursuance of the Ministry of Commerce notification No. SRO-49 (R)/66 dated the 23rd April, 1966, by or under any rule, order, notification and other instrument made or issued under this Imports and Exports (Control) Act, 1950. A point has been raised that since the Act of 1950 did not authorise the Government to impose the surcharge any rule, order, notification or other instrument imposing the surcharge can be declared invalid. The Act, as already found by us, did not empower the Government to impose the surcharge. It appears that to remove this lack of authority Act III of 1967 was enacted. Once the legislature has by enacting this Act, authorised the levy and imposition of price equalisation surcharge, no invalidity could attach to the levy or imposition of the surcharge. The only question that remains is whether after providings the necessary authority to impose the surcharge, Government action already taken on a wrong assumption of authority under a different Act, namely, the Act of 1950 can be validated, as has been sought to be done by the validation clause in section 7 of the Act III of 1967.
